To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the luminosity distribution of X-ray binaries can be used to infer the dynamical history and the star formation history of their host galaxies.
the observed luminosity distributions in X-ray binaries can be reproduced by the birth–death model.

the luminosity distributions (log N–log S curves) of X-ray binaries can be explained as the result of a simple birth–death process, that the birth rate of X-ray binaries varies as a function of time and of galactic location, and that the dynamical history and evolution of a galaxy can, at least in part, be inferred from its X-ray binary population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation, evolutionary history and dynamical history of X-ray binaries and the galaxies that host them.
the formation, evolution, and dynamical history of X-ray binaries and their host galaxies.
the formation of X-ray binaries, the formation of globular clusters, the dynamical evolution of galaxies and their components, the evolution of star clusters and the formation of planetary systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observed X-ray binary luminosity functions are the result of the dynamical history and the star formation history of the host galaxies, and the X-ray binary luminosities are a measure of the dynamical state of the galaxies.
the dynamical history and the star formation rate of a galaxy can both be traced by the luminosity distribution of its X-ray sources.
the dynamical history can be inferred by studying the luminosity distributions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the luminosity distributions and the evolution of the X-ray sources are the results of the interplay between the dynamical evolution of the host galaxies and the evolutionary history of the binaries.
the X-ray binaries in galaxies are the fossil records of their formation and dynamical history.
the X-ray luminosity functions of galaxies and their galactic components are determined by the birth–death processes of X-ray sources.
The main takeaway from our work is that
X-ray binary populations are excellent tools to probe the star-formation histories of galaxies.
, for the first time, the dynamical histories of galaxies can be reconstructed from the X-ray luminosity distributions of their X-ray binary populations.
the dynamical evolution of galaxies has a strong impact on the X-ray luminosity distributions of their X-ray binaries.
